newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU rift on China hinders treaty reform talks.
newsitem.headline: EU rift on China hinders treaty reform talks.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers, bickering over whether to condemn China's human rights record, will focus on technical internal reforms at a meeting in this Dutch coastal resort on Monday.

The bloc's 15 members, trying to agree sensitive reforms to be rubber-stamped at a mid-June Amsterdam summit, have struggled to find common ground on how to re-shape Union institutions ahead of an ambitious expansion into Eastern Europe.

In an attempt to streamline policy-making to suit a new era in which the bloc could have up to two dozen members within the next decade, ministers broadly agree that the existing 20-seat executive European Commission should be changed.
But there is a sharp divide over how many seats a revamped Commission should have. German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said there was "heated debate" on the issue on Sunday.

A French proposal for a sleek, effective 10-seat body, with all members guaranteed a seat on a five-year rotation basis, is fiercely opposed by the bloc's smaller nations, such as Ireland and the Scandinavians, who refuse to give up their national voice at the Brussels high table.
"We all agree we need a smaller, more efficient Commission, but the small- and medium-sized countries insist they keep their seats," Kinkel said.
The Dutch EU presidency summoned ministers to Noordwijk in a bid to inject fresh energy into the inter-governmental conference (IGC).
The Hague is concerned that the high-profile run-up to monetary union and trouble-spots like Albania have deflected attention away from setting the seal on wide-ranging reforms.
"The institutional questions are of vital importance for the success of the IGC," said Kinkel. "We need a solution so that enlargement can be possible."
Ministers will today tackle technical issues such as how member states' votes should be weighted during policy-making, giving fair representation to their respective populations.
Ministers fell out on Sunday over France's refusal to join an EU censure of China's human rights performance to be tabled at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo rounded on the double standards of some EU members in seeking to criticise smaller nations, such as Burma and Nigeria, over human rights but refusing to condemn larger, "commercially-important" nations.
The internal wrangling prompted Denmark to say it would table a motion against Beijing in Geneva this week. Diplomats said this had the backing of at least ten EU members.

Ministers, who last met only two weeks ago in Rome to celebrate the bloc's 40th birthday, will also turn their attention to Europe's 18 million jobless, discussing whether to include an employment chapter in a revised treaty.

The Dutch face a tight schedule to broker a revised treaty. If the IGC review is not completed by June, talks with those wanting to join the bloc will be delayed and risk becoming mired in crucial decisions on monetary union and in French and German elections next year.
